title: Lead: the rechargeable car battery

concepts.label: lead's three states: Pb / PbSO₄ / PbO₂
concepts.definition: Lead is stable at oxidation numbers 0 (grey metal Pb), +2 (white, insoluble, non-conducting lead sulfate PbSO₄) and +4 (brown, conducting lead dioxide PbO₂, a strong oxidising agent); the battery pairs the two outer states and both end in the middle one.

concepts.label: negative plate: Pb → PbSO₄
concepts.definition: On discharge spongy lead is oxidised, Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ (E° = −0.36 V as a reduction), and the insoluble sulfate stays stuck to the plate; this plate is the anode on discharge.

concepts.label: positive plate: PbO₂ → PbSO₄
concepts.definition: On discharge lead dioxide is reduced, PbO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O (E° = +1.69 V), again leaving solid lead sulfate on the plate; this plate is the cathode on discharge.

concepts.label: overall reaction: the acid is a reactant
concepts.definition: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O with n = 2: every electron through the wire removes one H₂SO₄ from the electrolyte and adds one H₂O, so the acid thins as the cell discharges.

concepts.label: 2.05 V per cell
concepts.definition: E°cell = 1.69 − (−0.36) = 2.05 V for one lead–acid cell (about 2.1 V rested with real battery acid), counted as a nominal 2 V.

concepts.label: cells in series
concepts.definition: Cells joined plus-to-minus in a chain so the same electrons pass through each in turn: voltages add (six lead–acid cells ≈ 12 V) while the ampere-hour capacity stays that of one cell.

concepts.label: state of charge
concepts.definition: The fraction of a battery's charge that is still available: 100% is full, 0% is flat.

concepts.label: acid density as fuel gauge
concepts.definition: Because sulfuric acid is consumed on discharge, the electrolyte density falls from about 1.28 g/mL (full) to about 1.12 g/mL (flat) and can be read with a hydrometer; rested cell voltage follows roughly as density + 0.84 V.

concepts.label: charging (electrons pushed backwards)
concepts.definition: An outside source with a voltage above the cell's own forces electrons into the negative plate and out of the positive plate, so both half-reactions run in reverse; anode and cathode swap, positive and negative plate do not.

concepts.label: reversible (rechargeable) cell reaction
concepts.definition: A cell reaction that can be run cleanly in both directions, here because the product PbSO₄ is a solid that stays on the plate where it formed: 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O ⇌ Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄.

concepts.label: overcharge / gassing
concepts.definition: Once the lead sulfate is used up (charging voltage above about 2.4 V per cell), the charging current splits water, 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (hydrogen at the negative plate, oxygen at the positive), losing about 0.34 g of water per Ah and producing an explosive gas mixture.

concepts.label: sulfation
concepts.definition: Lead sulfate left on the plates of a discharged battery coarsens into large, insulating crystals that can no longer be converted back, permanently reducing capacity; hence lead–acid batteries should be stored fully charged.

concepts.label: low Wh/kg, high current
concepts.definition: Lead gives only 2 electrons per 207 g (259 mAh/g), so lead–acid has about 170 Wh/kg in theory and 30–40 Wh/kg in practice, yet many thin porous plates and highly conducting acid let it deliver hundreds of amperes.

namedOnly: hydrometer (the float used to read acid density)
bisulfate HSO₄⁻ (real battery acid; the lesson uses the simplified SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ picture)
electrolysis (pointer: forcing a reaction uphill with an outside voltage)
slow electrode reactions / overpotential (why water does not split at 2.1 V; pointer to Real batteries, not named as overpotential)
internal resistance and voltage sag under load (pointer to Real batteries)
self-discharge (a few percent per month; taught properly in Nickel)
smart charger holding 14.4 V and letting the current fade (constant-voltage charging, not named)
molar volume of a gas, about 24.5 L/mol at room temperature (used once for the gas volume)
lithium cells as the lighter alternative (pointer)
summary: Running example: one cell of a 12 V, 60 Ah car battery, followed from Planté's 1859 idea (lead at 0, +2 and +4) through discharge (both plates become PbSO₄, 2.24 mol e⁻ consume 232 g Pb, 268 g PbO₂ and 220 g H₂SO₄), E° = 1.69 − (−0.36) = 2.05 V, six cells in series, acid density 1.28 → 1.12 g/mL as state-of-charge gauge (volts ≈ density + 0.84), charging as the reversed reaction, gassing (0.336 g water per Ah of overcharge, above about 2.4 V per cell), sulfation, and 'per kilogram of what?' (530 → 246 → 171 → 113 → about 35 Wh/kg). The capstone is a use-and-abuse simulator of that cell: headlights, smart or dumb charger, parking for months and topping up water, with animated electrons and ions, plate composition, acid density, hard sulfate and a battery-voltage trace. Hooks for later lessons: positive/negative plate vs anode/cathode swapping on charge, an electrolyte that is consumed (contrast with KOH in NiCd/NiMH), charging voltage must exceed cell voltage, water splitting as the side reaction that limits aqueous cells, self-discharge and capacity fade as ideas, and 30–40 Wh/kg as the baseline other chemistries are compared with.
